questions.question: Differentiate between cistron, muton and recon.
questions.solution_html:
• Cistron (2 marks).
  • A cistron is a functional unit of genetic material. It represents a segment of DNA containing a
  • sequence of nucleotides that controls a particular cellular function.
  • Important features
  • • A cistron is a functional unit of a gene.
  • • A protein-coding cistron begins with a start codon and ends with a termination (stop) codon.
  • • It generally contains the information required to produce one polypeptide chain.
  • Recon (1 mark).
  • A recon is the smallest unit of DNA capable of undergoing genetic recombination.
  • Features
  • • It is considered a unit of recombination.
  • • Recombination can occur between different recons within a genetic region.
  • Muton (1 mark)
  • A muton is the smallest unit of DNA capable of undergoing a mutation.
  • Features
  • • It is considered a unit of mutation.
  • • A muton may consist of one or more nucleotide pairs.
  • • A change in the nucleotide sequence of a muton can result in a mutation.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: • A change in the nucleotide sequence of a muton can result in a mutation.

questions.question: Describe the different methods of post translation modification of protein.
questions.solution_html:
• Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are chemical or structural changes that occur in proteins
  • after translation and help regulate their activity and stability.
  • Major types include
  • • Phosphorylation: Addition of phosphate groups, often regulating enzyme activity and cell
  • signalling.
  • • Glycosylation: Addition of carbohydrate groups, important in protein folding and cell
  • recognition.
  • • Acetylation: Addition of acetyl groups, which can regulate protein function and gene
  • expression.
  • • Methylation: Addition of methyl groups, involved in regulating histones and other proteins.
  • • Ubiquitination: Attachment of ubiquitin, often marking proteins for degradation.
  • • Proteolytic cleavage: Removal of specific peptide segments to activate proteins, as in the
  • conversion of proinsulin to insulin.
  • • Disulfide bond formation: Formation of bonds between cysteine residues that stabilize
  • protein structure. (Explain any four methods (4 marks).)

questions.question: Explain the A, P and E sites of ribosomes.
questions.solution_html:
• The ribosome contains three major tRNA-binding sites involved in translation.
  • A site (Aminoacyl site)
  • Receives the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA carrying the next amino acid.
  • P site (Peptidyl site)
  • Holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain. Peptide bond formation and chain transfer
  • occur during elongation.
  • E site (Exit site)
  • Temporarily holds the deacylated tRNA before it leaves the ribosome.
